prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its bioactive form, which established the incretin axis that underlies treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: All six openings put GLP-1 first, and I do not treat that agreement as the argument. The argument is that this is one of the few cases where a physiological concept, a gut hormone controlling insulin secretion, appetite and gastric emptying, was worked out in humans and then became a drug class with large outcome-trial benefit in diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal risk. The basic-science core (Holst on secretion and action of GLP-1 in humans, Drucker on receptor biology and the therapeutic rationale, Mojsov on identification of the bioactive peptide) fits a three-person limit and fits the Prize's emphasis on discovery with benefit to humankind. The evidence is mature, independently replicated and not likely to be revised.
statement.case_against: Credit is genuinely contested. Habener's group is not among the credited names although its role in the early peptide work is part of the priority dispute, and Mojsov's claim relative to that group rests on recollection that no one on this committee has verified. Excluding Knudsen means the prize honours the physiology and not the medicinal chemistry that produced liraglutide and semaglutide, so the citation must be worded carefully to avoid implying the committee is rewarding the drugs. Drug-class outcomes also remain incomplete on long-term safety, although I do not think that affects the case for the discovery.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks B010 first but flags Mojsov's priority against Habener as disputed and Knudsen's work as industrial development, and he ranks the unfolded protein response (B020) third as a clean, mechanistically complete two-person prize.
responses.response: I agree that the Mojsov question is the weak point of the GLP-1 trio, and I share his unease about leaving out the person who made the drugs. I would still keep Mojsov, because the bioactive truncated peptide is the step that turned proglucagon biology into a usable physiological signal. On B020 I agree that Mori and Walter are a clean pair, but I do not think it competes with B010 in 2026. The consequences for disease are real but mostly conceptual so far, whereas GLP-1 combines the concept with measured clinical outcomes. I keep B020 below my alternatives.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius would give B006 to June and Sadelain only, on the grounds that Rosenberg's decisive work is adoptive cell therapy broadly and that Eshhar's original CAR concept is not among the credited names.
responses.response: I find her narrowing of CAR-T to June and Sadelain more convincing than the three-name version I used in my opening. Rosenberg's claim is real but belongs to the wider field of T-cell therapy, and including him obscures what the prize would be rewarding. I disagree on one point. Removing Rosenberg does not solve the Eshhar problem, and a two-person CAR prize that omits the origin of the receptor concept is still vulnerable. I therefore regard B006 as a strong alternative but not one I would put ahead of GLP-1, and the attribution should be settled before it is chosen.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, favours a mix of molecular discovery (Nagel, Hegemann) and neuronal implementation (Deisseroth) for optogenetics, and ranks the nusinersen SMA work (B045) fourth for its neurological effect.
responses.response: I accept the molecular-plus-implementation split for B008, which is also my own. I would stress what it cannot fix: Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenbock all have credible claims, so any three-person version carries a priority dispute that will not go away. As a neuroscientist I use these tools, and I do not let that raise my ranking. For a prize in Physiology or Medicine the case for B008 is mainly methodological, with clinical use still at an early stage. On B045, I agree it is a clear mechanism-to-drug arc in a spinal motor-neuron disease, but I think it is a little early and may be read as recognition of antisense technology in general, so I leave it out of my alternatives.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks CAR-T second and the unfolded protein response third, and gives B008 only seventh place because therapeutic relevance to medicine is still limited.
responses.response: I agree with his reservation about B008 for a Physiology or Medicine prize, and it is the main reason I keep it as a second alternative and not as a co-laureate part alongside GLP-1. Where I disagree is on ranking CAR-T clearly ahead of optogenetics on medical grounds alone. CAR-T has the clearer clinical record, but its attribution is more fragile than he suggests, since the credited names omit Eshhar. Both alternatives carry a serious attribution problem, which is why I prefer a single settled GLP-1 prize to a two-part configuration that adds one of them.

uncertainties: Whether Habener and Knudsen can be accommodated in the citation or are better left out, given the three-person limit.
Whether Mojsov's priority over Habener's group survives scrutiny; none of us has verified it.
Whether the committee would prefer a two-part prize pairing GLP-1 with CAR-T, which the three-person limit would force into a different allocation of names.
Whether the Eshhar omission makes any CAR-T configuration unsafe.
statement.conflict_note: I co-authored a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons and I co-authored a 2019 review with Sten Grillner, who is not on this committee. Neither connection involves any shortlisted candidate or credited name, and no specific conflict requiring recusal is apparent from the provided profile.
